summary:
Andalucía stands under the national framework of Spain: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities and governs the regional position. Any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious in the parliamentary passage of the law.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry, so a visitor's operative basis for facility rules is the entry obtained through self-declaration rather than any medical documentation.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence, although discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics are defined and sanctioned under Ley 4/2023 itself.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Andalucía's own layer sits on top of that national floor and runs deeper than most Spanish regions. Ley 2/2014, an integral law for non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity, was among the first trans-specific regional laws in Europe. Ley 8/17 of 28 December, in force 4 February 2018, guarantees LGTBI rights and equal treatment for LGTBI people and their families. The regional government approved an equality strategy for 2024-2028 on 26 December 2024.
tangentialFactors:
With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay in comparative terms, and is recognised in international rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.

Andalucía carries much of Spain's LGBTQ mass tourism, concentrated in Mijas, Torremolinos and Seville. High visibility of gay and trans visitors in these resorts coexists with the national penal framework rather than replacing it, and the region's long-standing anti-discrimination statutes predate the national law by nearly a decade.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005, and Ley 4/2023 further strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples.
localsOnly:
Residents of Andalucía are covered by two regional statutes in addition to national law. Ley 2/2014 establishes integral non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity at the level of the autonomous community, and Ley 8/2017 of 28 December, in force from 4 February 2018, guarantees LGTBI rights and equal treatment for LGTBI people and their families. The regional equality strategy for 2024-2028 was approved by the Andalucian government on 26 December 2024.

Ley 4/2023 obliges public bodies and covered entities to collect discrimination data broken down by the causes the law covers, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances. It also combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing, which bears on resident access to transition-related care as well as to ordinary services.

Ley 4/2023 also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, a regime that applies to residents and to long-term residents alike rather than to short-stay visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents an Andalucian court applying the Article 22.4 transfobia aggravation; the two enforcement decisions on record, in Vigo and Valencia, are examples from other Spanish jurisdictions and illustrate the national pattern rather than regional practice.

Whether any provision of Ley 2/2014 or Ley 8/2017 has been amended, repealed or left unenforced following the entry into force of Ley 4/2023 is unresolved in these sources. The relationship between the two regional statutes and the national law is not sourced here.

Regional implementation detail for Andalucía, including which offices handle registry rectification requests, processing times, and whether any local facility rules depart from the registry-marker basis set nationally, is not sourced. Nor is there material on hate-crime reporting rates, police training, or outcomes for trans detainees in the community.

The content of the 2024-2028 equality strategy beyond its approval date is not stated in the inventory, so its specific targets for trans persons remain unverified.
